title: Moral education
sentences: They say: Who has Youth has the future.
And people fight for Youth, to imprint certain moral principles,
to drill in certain religious articles of faith, to acquire certain good habits.
Thus they believe they best secure the future of Youth and, in her, the future of Mankind.
But as that Youth gradually grows up, she notices that those principles among people are indeed professed,
those articles of faith preached there, those habits formally honoured there — yet none of these are made into reality, into life.
The child who was taught always to speak the truth loses its way in the politics of worldly wisdom,
first in its own house, where judgment of others differs so entirely according as those others are absent or present;
then in social life, where 'business' and 'career' set their own moral demands;
finally in statecraft and the art of war, where success is often bought only through cunning deception of the opposing party.
The child who was taught to love God above all things, also above Mammon, soon learns that its
educators did not mean this so literally.
When it wishes to give its money to God, this first makes its pious educators uneasy, then angry, finally hard.
Mammon can provide clothes and food and shelter and human honour better than God.
Honour God with the mouth, Mammon with the deed.
And the child who had already progressed beyond memorizing and echoing wordly swagger and wordly piety,
who had already made certain good habits its own — the habit, for instance,
of being the least — is later calmly exploited by greed and lust for power.
The world of adults, including that of church folk, proves to it a contest to become the greatest.
Worse still when moral education has not consisted in drilling and imprinting intellectual formulations as demands of life,
nor in accustoming oneself to practical virtues, but in sanctifying and strengthening the will;
when education might bring things so far
that the child found its sole salvation in a life full of love and truth, when sincerity and justice and devotion became its very being.
How could such a disposition move within society?
Justice?
No — serving persons and parties.
Right sacrificed to name, position, interest.
Devotion?
Provided that devotion does not touch personal and social sins.
It is as though one let a bird, bred and reared for a pure atmosphere, go stumbling through foul
muddy alleys.
It is as though one sent a fish into the sandy desert and said: swim.
People raise the child for a world that does not exist.
They endow it with inclinations which — if they develop — make its life a murderous struggle.
They prepare it for a society that will cast it out or consume it.
Who has Youth has the future?
Before this youth becomes the future, in slowly growing into the world of adults,
it will gradually be deformed and finally assimilated to the old environment.
Who has the future has Youth.
When the child, growing older, again and again enters a circle and an atmosphere in which moral demands are taken seriously,
taken ever more seriously, it will through the influence of its surroundings become continually and increasingly familiar with a moral way of life.
In artificial fish-breeding one sees so nicely how the little fish, as they grow, are moved from basin to basin,
yet each new basin offers more space, water, light and air — everything according to the needs of the animals.
The nimble swimmers are not placed in ever fouler water.
They receive anew, each time, conditions of life in which their material well-being is best promoted.
It may be no different in the upbringing of human children.
Create for them a moral milieu.
For this, however, it is necessary that the elders entrusted with the moral education of the young begin by working on themselves.
Make the grown good first, and then, through them, the little ones.
For those elders are the shapers of this moral milieu.
Children must learn what love of truth, forbearance, and goodwill are — not from parlour sermons, but from the conduct of Father and Mother in daily life.
Through daily contact with those virtues they must make them their own, as a matter of course.
When moreover those virtues are spoken of,
let that serve only to make clearer to the young what is demanded of them as well.
But the chief thing is that parents themselves give what they require of their children,
so that the family atmosphere does not hinder the children from acting according to ethical demands, and those demands are brought to the child through a living lesson.
So too in school children must not be made incapable of being truthful and loving their neighbour; from the teacher's personality,
from his bearing toward adults and children, ought to go forth an unceasing, penetrating preaching.
Where is the moral influence when the teacher, forbidding his pupils for instance
to quarrel, himself lives in enmity with his colleagues, himself quarrels with complaining,
reproachful parents, indeed even during the lesson addresses his pupils in a rough, wrangling tone?
Then he creates not only an immoral milieu through his own conduct, but aggra-
vates it through the hypocritical distinction between word and deed.
First let the teacher be good; then through him let the school youth grow.
And this applies not only to the primary-school teacher.
Also to those of the training school, the secondary school, the university.
What power can proceed from a pedagogy lesson that in the practice of the lesson itself already contradicts the theory proclaimed?
Pupils are taught to theorize about truths instead of being trained in realizing truths.
Thus they are taught to treat the seriousness of things lightly, if not to mock the holy.
A professor who says he loves science and is called convinced of the blessed influence of scientific civilization —
does he seize every lecture to show that love,
to pass it on, to plant that conviction in the minds and hearts of students?
Or will he alienate his hearers from science through dry dictated notes, through rote work,
and thereby undermine faith in its appeal and salutary influence?
Then improvement must begin with him.
And this is in the very first place true for those
who see themselves charged especially with the moral and religious formation of young and old.
From the Church, in all her manifestations, moral strength proceeds.
But then the Church must not be viewed as a Priesthood watching over a doctrine,
but as a Community of God-seekers, truly desiring sanctification, working for the moral welfare
of mankind.
How though, when the servants of that Church are not living proof of the power and blessedness of their preaching?
And when also the laypeople who gather around them
are not living messengers of the salvation of truth, 'living letters of Christ'?
Then the salt has lost its savour.
And wherewith shall it be salted?
People are always so concerned about the salvation of youth.
Rightly so.
But whoever is truly concerned about it, let him begin by making of himself morally the best he can.
Then he has already worked seriously on one factor of moral education — the foremost.
Then he has helped create a pure atmosphere in which the young birds must learn to fly.
Begin with the adults; begin with ourselves.
Had Jesus Christ not begun with Himself, the blessing of Christianity would never have become our portion.
And when that blessing is not far greater, it is because we fail,
empowered by Him, to follow His example herein and to begin with ourselves.
I wrote this piece at the request of the Bureau for the 'Congress for Moral Education'.
Our readers will see nothing new in it.
Yet it seemed useful to remind us adults that the seriousness of our striving must show in our deeds.
A child may not swallow a gnat, and we adults strain at camels.
